messages.mes:
The staff had a modest weight to it, a faint warmth in the grain where his hand settled, as if the wood had been sitting in the sun. The fields stayed behind him. Ahead, carts and foot traffic thickened along the road, and Alderwatch's walls rose gray and patched with moss, tall enough that the morning light had not yet cleared their shadow from the gate.

He kept to the side, and the road taught him its habits. A woman leading a donkey loaded with firewood nodded to the gate guards and passed without slowing. Two men with plows over their shoulders argued about rain. Nobody looked twice at a young man in plain robes with a staff, and the guards under the arch glanced at him once, filed him among the morning traffic, and went back to their talk. The gate swallowed him into noise: wheels on stone, a smith's hammer somewhere close, the smell of bread and horse dung and wet mortar.

Inside, the street opened onto a market front with awnings and a crooked sign showing a fish. People moved with places to be. He caught a man in a leather apron carrying a crate toward a doorway, ordinary middle years, flour dusted on one sleeve.

"Excuse me — could you point me to the Adventurers' Guild?"

The man set the crate down on his hip and looked him over, robes to staff to face.

"Guild? Straight up this street, past the well, and it's the big stone hall on your left with the crossed swords carved over the door. Can't miss it." He shifted the crate. "Sign-in desk's on the ground floor, if that's what you're after. They'll want your two silver ready."

messages.mes:
The street climbed gently past the well, where a queue of buckets and chatter clogged the cobbles, and the Guild hall stood exactly as promised: a broad stone face, dark timber door, crossed swords chiseled deep above the lintel. He stopped at the threshold and let his eyes do the walking first.

Inside was one large open floor, cooler than the street and smelling of lamp oil, old paper and boot leather. To the right, a long notice board hung heavy with parchment slips, arranged in rows, a cluster of people standing before it with their heads tilted. To the left, tables and benches where a few adventurers sat over breakfast and gear — a woman fletching arrows, two men arguing quietly over a map. Farther back, a heavy counter where someone was weighing what looked like a bundle of claws. The sign-in desk sat near the door itself, a plain oak thing with a bell, manned by a clerk with gray at her temples and a ink-stained cuff.

He crossed the floor. Her eyes came up from a ledger.

"Good morning. I'd like to register as an adventurer. What do you need from me, and what's the fee? I was told two silver — is that right?"

"Two silver, correct. One-time." She pulled a fresh page toward her and dipped a pen. "Name, age, and which Class you'll declare — the stone reads your Rank after, that part's not up to you. You'll sign the roll, take the Guild's terms — no stealing from clients, no brawling in the hall, contracts are honored or they're paid for." She set the pen down within his reach and slid a small brass tray across the wood. "Two silver in the tray, then we start. Any questions before you commit?"

The two silver clicked into the tray. The clerk counted them with one glance, swept them into a drawer, and turned the ledger toward him. He signed. The ink dried while she rose and beckoned him along the counter to a waist-high stone pillar set into the wall behind the desk, its top worn smooth and pale where a thousand hands had rested it.

"Hand flat on the stone. It does the rest."

The stone was cool, then not. A faint tingle ran up his arm, and a dull amber glow bloomed under his palm, steady, unremarkable. The clerk read it without ceremony.

"Rank F. That's your measured strength — separate thing from your Guild standing. You're Novice with us." She fetched a small metal plate from a drawer, stamped with the Guild's crossed swords and a fresh number, still cool from the metal. "Carry that. Any branch honors it. Losses cost you." She set it on the desk beside the ledger and nodded toward the board. "Novice work's the bottom two rows. Take a slip to me if you want one made active — the contract's only live once I book it."

The board was thick with parchment. Down at the bottom two rows, the slips marked for Novices read:

**Cull the Burial Gallery Skeletons** — client: Temple Wardens of Alderwatch · reward: 120 cp · Clear the restless dead from level 1 of the Old Crown Catacombs beneath the ruined chapel so the wardens can resume patrols of the burial galleries.

**Thin the Millpond Snappers** (4) — client: Hessa Crowder, miller at Crowder's Mill · reward: 60 cp · Kill four mud snappers in the millpond and millrace so the millwheel can turn without fouling its gears.

**Shepherd the Dyers' Cart** — client: Alderwatch Dyers' Guildhall · reward: 90 cp · Escort the dyers' mule cart carrying three bolts of finished woad cloth to the market hamlet of Thornford; word of waylayers on the river road has the drivers afraid to travel alone.

**Medicine for the Quarry Camp** — client: Greldin the Herbalist · reward: 40 cp · Carry a sealed satchel of feverfew tincture and bone-set dressings to the quarry foreman at Graybank stone quarry before the fever there spreads further.

**Drive Off the Coop Raiders** — client: Bram Tolliver, goose farmer at Tolliver Stead · reward: 70 cp · Identify and stop whatever has been breaking into the goose pens each night, by killing it or driving it off, so the remaining flock survives to market.

The clerk had gone back to her ledger, pen scratching.

messages.mes:
She took the slip, read it, and set it flat on the desk without stamping yet.

"Number first. The Temple doesn't count bones, they count quiet. The job's done when level one has no restless dead left walking it — the wardens go back down on patrol behind you and if their priests find nothing stirring, that's cleared. Kill three and leave three rattling in a side gallery, they'll send it back to you unpaid. Do it thorough and you won't hear from them at all." She tapped the slip. "The Guild seal on there turns ready once the outcome's established. No trophies to carry back, no bodies to show. The wardens' own word down there does the proving."

She pulled a rough map sheet from a drawer beneath the counter, unfolded it against the wood, and set one ink-stained fingernail west of the city walls.

"Entrance is under the ruined chapel of Old Crown — old burial site, older than the walls here. It's a bit over an hour out by the west road, cart track for the last stretch, chapel on a low rise where the fields give out. Road's safe enough this time of day; it's a working road, quarry traffic and farmers on it. The danger's all under the floor." She straightened. "First level's the shallow end — that's why it's Novice work. If you go down a stair and find the dead wearing armor and moving in order, that's level two, and that's not your contract. Come back up."

She inked her stamp, pressed it to the slip, and slid it across to him, the Guild seal fresh and red beside the written terms.

"Booked active. Bring the slip back to any branch desk when it's done and you're paid — one hundred and twenty copper, posted and guaranteed." She was already reaching for her ledger again. "Anything else, or are you off to go grave-robbing the honest way?"

"West gate." She tilted her pen toward the door. "Straight down the market street the way you came, through the square, and the west gate's the one with the wool merchants' sheds outside it. You'll see the carts."

She sat back and rubbed a smudge of ink off her knuckle with her thumb, considering the second question the way a person considers whether to save someone money.

"The Guild doesn't sell draughts. Nearest apothecary is Marrow's, two doors down from the well you passed — green hanging sign, smells like a wet garden. For wounds you want a stitched and dressed kit, maybe a vial of the red salve if he trusts you not to drink it. For mana—" she gave him a brief once-over, staff and robes and all, "—he'll call it azure tincture, and it'll cost you real silver, not copper. Fresh Novice on his first job, I'd tell you the truth: a mana draught's dear, and level one of Old Crown is a long day's cull, not a sprint. If you know your own limits you can walk out before you're empty. But it's your coin, and it's your bones down there."

The hall carried on behind her — the fletching woman bit a thread, the two map men pushed a wooden marker across their chart. The clerk dipped her pen again.

"That's everything from me. Good luck, Novice Red. Desk's here till sundown if the dead disagree with you."

messages.mes:
The well square was busier than it had been an hour ago — a woman scrubbing the trough lip, two carters arguing over a space — and the green sign hung two doors down, paint flaking, the smell reaching him before the door did. Dried herbs, vinegar, something bitter underneath. Inside, bundles hung from the rafters on strings, jars crowded a shelf behind the counter, and a stooped man with soil-stained nails was grinding something in a mortar. He looked up at "Master Marrow" without hurrying.

"Marrow. Who sent you?"

He listened to the rest with the mortar still turning under his pestle, then set it down and came to the counter, wiping his hands on his apron.

"Guild sends me their new ones when they can afford me and think they can't. Right, the damage." He held up fingers one at a time. "Stitched and dressed kit — bandages boiled, needle, thread, the red salve in a small pot — six coppers. That's the honest one, buy it. Red salve on its own, same pot, four coppers. Smear it on a cut, not a feast; a pot like that closes a wound and keeps the rot out, but it's not a healer in a jar. Bleeding's still bleeding until you bind it."

For the azure tincture he walked the shelf, pulled a squat dark vial, and set it down without letting go of it.

"One silver and eight coppers, and that's me being fair. One vial puts back what a man your size spends in a hard fight — a good bolt, a lance, a few lesser workings — and it takes effect slow, a minute or two, not a gulp and back to full. It's not a jug of wine. One vial. That's what I stock for Novices."

He folded his hands on the counter and looked at Alaric over the three vials and pots laid out between them.

"Three silver, you said. So: kit and the tincture, you walk out with one silver and six coppers and everything a first trip under Old Crown could ask of an apothecary. Kit alone, you keep two silver and change and you mind your mana the way the clerk told you. Your coin. Which is it?"

messages.mes:
The ground told its story plainly enough once he looked. The trampled yard wore boot prints — several sets, recent, coming and going in pairs, the regular tread of men who walked this ground on a schedule. At the chapel mouth the pattern changed: a wider drag-mark scored through the dust of the threshold, bone-pale scratches on the worn sill, and a scatter of dry fragments — not whole bones, chips and flakes of them — trailing a few feet down the first steps before the wind and rain had thinned it out. Something had come up as far as the light and been dragged or driven back down. The prints of the wardens' patrols crossed over it and over it again, weeks of coming and going, and none of the boots had gone deeper than the stair head in a long while.

He went down with his hand on the wall.

The stair was honest work, old but sound, each step dished in the middle by centuries of feet. The light of the yard gave out after a dozen steps and the dark took on a smell — cold stone, old earth, the dry dusty sweetness of things long dead. His boots sounded loud. He learned the rhythm of it: step, listen, step. Water had once run somewhere below; a slow drip kept its own count off in the dark, patient as the dead.

The stair ended in a long gallery.

It ran away to his left and right in a low vaulted corridor, ceiling close enough to touch with the staff, walls of fitted stone pierced by burial niches from floor to shoulder height — dozens of them, most holding only a few dry bones and the dust of the rest. Two or three lamps of black horn hung from iron hooks, unlit. Silt and bone-dust softened the floor. Down the gallery to the left, at the far edge of what his eyes could make out in the grey seep from the stair, something shifted.

Not shifted — turned. Three figures stood in the passage perhaps forty feet off, and one of them was rotating its head toward him, a slow dry grind of bone on bone, sockets finding the sound of his boots. They had been standing among the niches like men at their own graves, and they were not standing like that now. Ribs yellowed through gaps in rot-bitten casing, limbs thin but unhurried, fingers like bundles of dry sticks flexing once. The nearest took a first clattering step, and the other two came with it, three sets of bone feet finding a rhythm on the stone, closing the distance at a shuffling walk that did not look like it intended to stop.

messages.mes:
The three came on without hurry, and the hurry was the problem — no stumble in them, no hesitation at the light. Bone feet found their rhythm on the stone, and the gallery gave back the clatter doubled, so he could not tell how many walked behind him until the sockets swung his way and it was only the three. They closed the dark between them at that patient shuffle, fingers opening and closing, the smallest of the three in the lead with its jaw working loosely against its own spine.

He leveled the staff.

The lance went from his hand as a hiss of orange that shoved the gloom back the length of the gallery, and it took the smallest one square in the chest. Fire filled the rib cage from inside — one instant of a lit lattice, every yellowed bone thrown sharp in its own glow — and then the casing burst, dry fragments and burning slivers of rot-bitten wrapping spraying across the niches. What hit the floor was a scatter of blackened sticks and a skull that rolled twice and stopped, sockets smoking. The smell of burnt dust and old fat flooded the corridor.

The other two did not pause to consider it. The big one and the last — broader through the shoulders, its bones darker, older, with a helm's rotten band still crusted to its skull — came straight over their fallen fellow's remains, and they closed the ground his lance's flash had opened up again. Ten feet. Less. The big one's finger bones flexed once, and it raised its arm, and there was nothing casual in the way it did it now.

They were on him, both of them, close enough that the cold coming off them touched his face.

The lance caught the big one square in the crust of its old helm-band, and the fire went through it like wind through a reed fence — a burst that lit every niche in the gallery and blew a rain of burning fragments off its shoulders and arms. The thing rocked under it, casing scorched black across the chest, one arm hanging in loose splinters, and still it stood. Still it came. Badly broken now, bones showing through burned wrapping, but the sockets found him and the legs drove it across the stone at him without a sound but the clatter.

He gave the half-step and it ate the distance anyway, arm swinging before he fully set his foot. The blow came low and he turned the staff into it too late — the cold force cracked across his ribs and side, a hard blunt hammer of a hit that drove the air half out of him and spun him a step toward the stair-wall. Pain spread under his ribs, deep and hot, and his breath came back in a hiss.

The skeleton was still on him — engaged, close, cold pouring off its broken frame, the splintered arm twitching at its side while the good one gathered itself. The dark of the gallery behind it held nothing but the drip of water and the smell of burnt dust.

The swing never landed. The lance went through the broken chest before the good arm reached its height, and the fire blew the scorched casing apart from within — the whole frame bursting into a last spray of blackened slivers that rattled off the stair-wall and his shoulders. The skull struck the stone, rolled against his boot, and lay with its sockets smoking. The cold pouring off the thing died with it, and the gallery's own chill, older and quieter, closed back in.

Then nothing. His own breathing, ragged under the ache in his ribs. Water dripping somewhere down the dark of the gallery. The tick of cooling bone.

He held at the stair-mouth and listened. No clatter of more bone feet. No rasp of fingers along a niche. The dark ran on past the three scatterings of remains into a black the staff-glow's memory could not reach, and whatever it held was keeping quiet, or keeping still, or keeping its distance.

His side throbbed with each breath, deep and blunt, and his forearm where the first blow had landed carried a numb ache that was only now beginning to warm into ordinary pain. The magic pouch at his hip sat heavier with what the fight had left him — pale bones, a small quantity of grave dust — though the weight it carried was more accounting than burden.

The way out stood behind him, up the worn steps to the chapel air. The gallery ran on ahead, down toward the deeper dark, toward whatever else the wardens' contract had not yet named.

messages.mes:
The kit came open on his knees: boiled bandages still stiff from the roll, needle and thread he was glad not to need, the little pot of red salve with its smell of tallow and something bitter underneath. He worked the salve into his side where the blow had landed, pressing until the bruise flared and then dulled under the grease, and wound a bandage tight around the forearm, pinning the end with practiced turns. The wax came off the azure vial with a crack of the thumb. It tasted of cold river water and, faintly, of iron.

Then he sat and gave it its three minutes, staff across his knees, watching the light-line where the chapel's grey morning fell down the steps and died on the gallery floor.

The shaking in his fingers went first. Then the deep ache under his ribs loosened its grip, breath by breath, warmth spreading through the bandaged places like water through dry cloth. The cold of the gallery stopped reaching his bones. By the last minute he could fill his lungs all the way down, and the forearm answered when he flexed it, sore but his own.

He rose, tested his weight, and went down the gallery one niche at a time.

Quiet steps, staff up. Past the first scatter of burnt bone, past the second, where the skull still lay against the wall with its sockets dark. The niches on either side held their old dead in stillness — no twitch of wrapping, no rasp. Water dripped somewhere ahead. The gallery bent left, and the bend opened into a wider room where the ceiling climbed and the dark sat differently, broken by a seam of faint blue along the far wall.

The room had been a resting place for somebody better buried than the rest. A stone bier stood on a raised step at its center, swept clean by no living hand, its occupant long gone. In the wall behind it, the blue seam ran floor to ceiling in a shallow arch — a sealed way down, cold to look at, stone fitted so close he could not have found the joint without the glow. Old carvings crowded the arch's face, worn smooth at their edges, and the dust on the bier's step held no tracks but his own.

messages.mes:
The carvings gave up their shape slowly from a staff's length: a border of kneeling figures, worn nearly to suggestion, framing the arch like bearers at a coffin. Whatever words had run along the arch's crown were gone past reading. The blue came from the seam itself, a cold light with no source he could find, and the air within a hand's breadth of it carried a different chill than the gallery's — still, settled, patient. No keyhole, no lever, no hinge. The stone had been set to be set, and opening it would want either force he did not have or knowledge of a working he had never been taught. He left it its secrets.

The sweep back up the gallery he did slowly, staff up, niche by niche.

He found what the dark had hidden from him the first time, at the third branch past the bend — a side passage, narrow, its mouth shaded by the corner's angle so that from the stair it had read as solid wall. The floor told on it anyway: a drag-mark through the dust, old but plain, bone-ends and small stones scored in a line leading in. The dust inside lay otherwise undisturbed, and the air coming out of the passage smelled different — not the gallery's old stone but something sharper underneath, like a cellar where meat had been kept.

The passage ran back perhaps twenty paces to a low chamber where the staff-glow's edge caught pale heaps along the walls: bones, sorted, not scattered. Skulls in one stack, long bones in another, stacked with a care nothing in this gallery had shown so far. Between the heaps, a shape sat against the far wall in the dark, robed in what might once have been winding-cloth, still as furniture. It did not move while he watched. It did not need to be moving to be waiting.

Beyond it, the chamber's back wall held a second drag-mark in the dust, fresher, running out of the chamber toward a crack of deeper dark — and somewhere down that dark, faint but real, came the slow scrape of something dragging bone on stone.

messages.mes:
The points settled in him the way weight settles in a ship taking cargo — nothing visible, but everything a shade steadier. The mana behind his breastbone sat deeper, wider, like a well refilled past its old waterline. He flexed his fingers around the staff and the ache in his skull from the lance's recoil had gone quiet.

The drag-mark led him across the chamber floor, and he walked it the way he'd promised himself: slow, staff up, a stop every few paces with his ear turned toward the crack. The scrape came again while he listened — closer now, or the dark just carried better — a wet-ish rattle of bone over stone, unhurried. Nothing answered his voice. Between the bone heaps the dust held other tracks, older ones, small and claw-toed, coming and going from the crack in a worn path.

The crack itself was wider than it had looked from the passage mouth, a split in the masonry a body could shoulder through, breathing cold air. Old scratch-marks furred its edges, layered deep, the way a doorpost gets marked by a knife-check kept for years.

He was still three paces out when the scrape stopped.

Then stone clacked, and it came out — not crawling, as its dragging sound had promised, but walking, badly, a skeleton in the tatters of what had been a warden's tabard, grey cloth gone to rot over bone gone yellow-brown. It carried a rusted bill-hook in one hand, and where its skull should have tilted to look at him, it simply turned, jaw hanging, eye sockets full of the blue glow he'd seen at the arch's seam. It stopped in the crack's mouth, filled it, and raised the bill-hook to its shoulder with a creak of dry tendon.

It didn't charge. It stood there, waiting on him, the way a sentry waits.
